name: Countering
html:
🖼️ Framing Our Work

In this module, we will take a closer look at the move of countering. As students begin to consider multiple perspectives on a topic or issue, they will certainly encounter sources with which they disagree. With practice over time, students can learn to focus less on disagreement and more on offering alternatives and new ways of thinking. In more sophisticated arguments, countering is less about pointing to an opposing view and more about analyzing different viewpoints to understand their goals and limitations.

In Writing Rhetorically: Fostering Responsive Thinkers and Communicators, Jennifer Fletcher has this to say about writing counterarguments:

Should we teach students to automatically rebut opposing views? How about this instead: Let’s teach students to engage the reasoning; understand the reasoning; challenge or extend or complicate the reasoning; and when appropriate, perhaps rebut the reasoning. If we want collective decision-making and civic participation not log jammed by partisan feuds then we shouldn’t teach rebuttal as the default response to diverse perspectives (Fletcher, 113).

Fletcher’s perspective on countering is in line with Joseph Harris’s argument that “to counter is not to nullify but to suggest a different way of thinking.” This is important to keep in mind as you work through this chapter. Unlike a debate where two sides are pitted against each other when countering in an argument, new lines of inquiry are opened.

🔎 Explore and Learn

In all his purposes for countering, Harris stresses the constructive nature of countering and goes beyond a simple point/counterpoint understanding. Instead, when writers counter other texts, they do so in order to advance their own point of view. We want student writers to carefully and respectfully consider all reasonable perspectives on an issue, including perspectives they may not agree with, before joining the conversation.

Harris sees three main approaches for countering:

  • Arguing the other side: Showing the usefulness of a term or idea that a writer has criticized or noting problems with one that she or he has argued for.

  • Uncovering values: Surfacing a word or concept for analysis that a text has left undefined or unexamined.

  • Dissenting: Identifying a shared line of thought on an issue in order to note its limits (58)

Teaching Tip: Elementary students may find it helpful to spend time exploring and trying on each type of countering move before purposefully making decisions on using the moves.

Check out this slideshow to see examples of the three countering moves:

To further explore countering and see additional examples, check out this slideshow below. This resource also includes some language for making the move.

Try and Share

Now, let’s take a look at some student examples of countering moves.

Make a copy of the Making Moves with Evidence: Countering Student Samplesdocument. Then, read the student examples and add annotations in the notes column to describe the counteringmove the student writer is trying out. What choices did the writer make about how to use the evidence?

💬 Reflect and Share

Reflect on your learning about countering and share your thoughts in the discussion.

  • How did this chapter extend or change your thinking about countering?

  • Reflect on your own experience with countering. Share a time when you used one of these countering moves effectively. Or, think about a time you could have used one of the moves to make a more effective argument.

Continue the conversation by responding to others’ posts about countering moves and how you might support this work with your students.
